gloss: roll, roll away; what is rolled or round: heap, wave, scroll, wheel, skull, bowl
summary: To roll: a stone from the mouth of a well or to the mouth of a cave, the heavens rolled up like a scroll, justice rolling on like waters, a garment rolled in blood, and in a figure to roll one's way or works onto Yahweh, committing them to him. Its nouns are things rolled or round: גַּל a heap of stones or a wave of the sea, מְגִלָּה a scroll, גַּלְגַּל a wheel or whirl, גֻּלְגֹּלֶת a skull (Golgotha), גֻּלָּה a bowl or basin, and the place names Gilgal, where Yahweh “rolled away” the reproach of Egypt, and Galilee, “the circuit”. בִּגְלַל is “on account of”. The Aramaic and Syriac roll, wave, wheel and skull, Akkadian galālu “roll”, gulgullu “skull” and gullu “bowl”, and Arabic jallah “a lump of dung” and min jalalika “for your sake” match its words.

words.summary: Forty-eight times, only in the plural and with suffixes, thirty-nine of them in Ezekiel: Israel's idols, things it set up in its heart and went after, and by which it was made unclean. The link to the root is not clear. The word is pointed like שִׁקּוּץ “detestable thing”, with which it is paired (Deu 29:16; Ezk 20:7), and it sounds like גֶּלְלֵי “dung” (Ezk 4:12, 15), so it may be a scornful name, “dung-things”; or it may name shapeless rolled blocks. No verse or cognate settles which, and no cognate names idols by this root.

senses.gloss: idols, false gods and their images
senses.definition: The images and gods Israel served instead of Yahweh, named with contempt, beside “abominations” and “detestable things”; they defile those who go after them, and Yahweh will cleanse Israel from them.

evidence.note: “They served הַגִּלֻּלִים, of which Yahweh had said to them, You shall not do this thing.”
“You saw their detestable things (שִׁקּוּצֵיהֶם) and their גִּלֻּלֵיהֶם, wood and stone, silver and gold, which were among them.”
“I will pile your corpses on the corpses of your גִּלּוּלִים”: dead things like their worshippers.
Ahab “did very abominably in going after the גִּלֻּלִים, as the Amorites did”.
“These men have brought up their גִּלּוּלִים on their heart”: idols held in the heart, not only set up in a shrine.
“Cast away every man the detestable things of his eyes, and do not defile yourselves with the גִּלּוּלִים of Egypt.”
“You have become guilty by your blood that you shed, and defiled by your גִּלּוּלִים that you made.”
“From all your גִּלּוּלִים I will cleanse you.”
“They shall no longer defile themselves with their גִּלּוּלִים.”
The idols of Babylon: “Bel is put to shame … her גִּלּוּלֶיהָ are dismayed.”

evidence.locator: Ezk.14.3; Ezk.36.25, גִּלּוּלִים → εἴδωλα (also ἐνθυμήματα, ἐπιτηδεύματα elsewhere in Ezekiel)

evidence.note: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.”
“What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” followed by Ezk 37:27 and Lev 26:12.

parallels.note: Detestable thing; set beside the idols.

words.gloss: Gilgal, “rolling”, where Yahweh rolled away the reproach of Egypt
words.summary: Israel's first camp in the land, east of Jericho, where the twelve stones from the Jordan were set up, the men born in the wilderness were circumcised, and the first Passover in the land was kept. Scripture gives the name its meaning: “Today I have rolled away (גַּלּוֹתִי) the reproach of Egypt from you, and the name of that place is called Gilgal.” It was later a place of Samuel's circuit and of Saul's kingship, and in Hosea and Amos a shrine of false worship; another Gilgal lay on the border of Judah (Jos 15:7), and Beth-gilgal near Jerusalem (Neh 12:29).

senses.definition: The place by Jericho named from Yahweh's rolling away of Israel's reproach, Israel's camp in the conquest and later a centre of worship and of the kingdom.

evidence.note: “Today I have rolled away (גַּלּוֹתִי) the reproach of Egypt from upon you. So the name of that place is called גִּלְגָּל to this day.”
The people came up from the Jordan and camped in Gilgal; Joshua set up there the twelve stones.
The Passover kept at Gilgal in the plains of Jericho.
Joshua and all Israel returned to the camp at Gilgal.
Samuel's yearly circuit: Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah.
There they made Saul king before Yahweh in Gilgal.
Elijah and Elisha went from Gilgal.
“All their evil is in Gilgal, for there I hated them.”
“Gilgal shall surely go into exile (הַגִּלְגָּל גָּלֹה יִגְלֶה)”: a play on the name.
“From Shittim to Gilgal, that you may know the righteous acts of Yahweh”: the crossing of the Jordan remembered.
A Gilgal on the border of Judah, opposite the ascent of Adummim; Jos 18:17 calls it Geliloth.
Beth-gilgal (בֵּית הַגִּלְגָּל), a village of the singers.

words.gloss: heap (of stones), ruin-heap; wave, billow; spring
words.summary: Something rolled up together: a heap of stones raised as a witness or over the dead, a city made a heap of ruins, and the waves of the sea that roll up and roll on. Sng 4:12 גַּל נָעוּל “a locked spring”, beside “a sealed fountain”, is a spring or pool, as גֻּלָּה is. The brief's count includes Isa 10:30 (Gallim) and the token of Psa 119:22, which is the verb.

senses.gloss: heap of stones; heap of ruins
senses.definition: A heap of stones piled up as a witness or memorial, or over a dead man's body; and a city or house thrown down into heaps.

evidence.note: “Jacob said to his brothers, Gather stones; and they took stones and made a גַּל.”
“This גַּל is a witness between me and you today.”
“This heap is a witness and the pillar is a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you.”
“They raised over him a great heap of stones to this day”: over Achan.
Over the king of Ai.
Over Absalom in the pit in the forest.
“You have made of a city a heap (לַגָּל), of a fortified town a ruin.”
“I will make Jerusalem heaps (לְגַלִּים), a lair of jackals.”
“Babylon shall become heaps.”
Fortified cities laid waste into ruinous heaps (Isa 37:26).
“Their altars shall be like heaps on the furrows of the field.”
The roots of the godless “wrap around a heap”.

senses.definition: The waves of the sea, which rise and roar and roll over; Yahweh raises them, sets their bounds and stills them.

evidence.note: “He spoke and raised a stormy wind, which lifted up its waves (גַּלָּיו).”
“He made the storm a calm, and their waves were still.”
“Thus far you shall come and no further, and here shall your proud waves be stayed.”
The sand set as the bound of the sea: “its waves toss but cannot prevail; they roar but cannot pass over it.”
“You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them.”
“I am Yahweh your God, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar.”
“All your breakers and your waves have gone over me.”
Jonah in the deep uses the same words.
“Your righteousness like the waves of the sea”: unceasing.
“Many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.”
He will strike the waves in the sea, as at the exodus.
The boat covered by the waves; the Peshitta's ܓܠܠܐ.

senses.definition: A spring of water, in the Song a locked spring, beside a sealed fountain.

evidence.note: “A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a גַּל locked, a fountain (מַעְיָן) sealed.”
“Wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame.”
“Then they will say … to the hills, Cover us”: the Greek word only, from Hos 10:8, not this Hebrew.

parallels.note: The pillar set up with the heap as a second witness.

phrases.gloss: a great heap of stones (over the dead)

words.gloss: roll, roll away; be rolled up; roll oneself upon; commit (one's way) to
words.summary: About twenty times, in seven stems. A thing rolled is turned over and over along the ground: a great stone, the heavens like a scroll, a body in blood, water in a stream. Its figure is to roll a load off oneself onto another: “roll your way upon Yahweh” is to commit it to him and trust him (Psa 37:5, parallel “trust in him”). The brief's no-stem tokens are the noun גַּל “heap”, filed here by spelling. Psa 119:22 גַּל “roll away from me reproach” is listed as a piel but is the imperative as at Jos 5:9's “roll away reproach”; it is kept here under the qal.

stems.gloss: roll (a stone); roll away; roll onto, commit to

senses.definition: To roll a heavy stone: from the mouth of a well to water the flock, or to the mouth of a cave to shut it.

evidence.note: “They would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place.”
Jacob alone rolled the stone from the well's mouth for Rachel.
“Roll great stones to the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them.”
“Roll a great stone to me today”: for slaughtering properly, the blood drained.
“He who rolls a stone, it will come back on him.”

senses.definition: To roll a burden of shame off someone and take it away.

evidence.note: “Today I have rolled away (גַּלּוֹתִי) the reproach of Egypt from upon you”: when the men born in the wilderness had been circumcised.
“Roll from upon me (גַּל מֵעָלַי) reproach and contempt, for I have kept your testimonies.”

senses.definition: To roll one's way, works or cause onto Yahweh: to hand them over to him and leave them with him in trust.

evidence.note: “Roll your way upon Yahweh, and trust in him, and he will act”: rolling is set beside trusting.
“Roll your works to Yahweh, and your plans will be established.”
The mockers: “He rolled (it) to Yahweh; let him deliver him, let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
The chief priests at the cross: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he desires him”: Psa 22:9 with גֹּל as “he trusted”.

senses.definition: Of the heavens, to be rolled up as a scroll is rolled, put away from sight.

evidence.note: “All the host of the heavens shall rot away, and the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll (כַסֵּפֶר).”
“The heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled up”: the same picture.

senses.definition: Of waters, to roll on in a stream without ceasing.

evidence.note: “Let justice roll on like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.”

senses.definition: Of a soldier's garment, rolled over and over in blood in the battle.

evidence.note: “Every boot of the trampling warrior and every garment rolled (מְגוֹלָלָה) in blood will be for burning.”

senses.definition: To roll oneself onto someone, to fall upon and overwhelm him.

evidence.note: Joseph's brothers: “to roll himself upon us and fall upon us, and take us as slaves.”

senses.definition: To lie rolling in one's own blood.

evidence.note: “Amasa lay wallowing (מִתְגֹּלֵל) in his blood in the middle of the highway.”

senses.definition: To roll something down from a height.

evidence.note: Against Babylon, the destroying mountain: “I will stretch out my hand against you and roll you down (וְגִלְגַּלְתִּיךָ) from the crags.”

senses.definition: Of attackers, to roll in like a flood through a breach.

evidence.note: “As through a wide breach they come; amid the ruin they roll on (הִתְגַּלְגָּלוּ).”

evidence.locator: Gen.29.3, וְגָלֲלוּ → ἀπεκύλιον; Gen.29.8 → ἀποκυλίσωσιν; Gen.29.10 → ἀπεκύλισεν

evidence.note: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the door of the tomb?” … the stone had been rolled away.
An angel of the Lord rolled back the stone.
“As a scroll being rolled up (ἑλισσόμενον)”.
The quotation of Psa 22:9 uses πέποιθεν “he trusted”.

parallels.note: Trust: rolling one's way on Yahweh is trusting him.

phrases.gloss: roll (it) to Yahweh: commit (one's cause) to Yahweh

words.summary: A rolled book, a sheet written on and rolled up: Jeremiah's scroll that Jehoiakim cut and burned, the scroll Ezekiel ate, Zechariah's flying scroll, and “the scroll of the book” in which it is written of the one who comes to do Yahweh's will. Often מְגִלַּת סֵפֶר “a scroll of a book”. The brief's count includes Ezr 6:2, which is the Aramaic word.

senses.definition: A roll for writing on, unrolled to be read column by column, and rolled up again.

evidence.note: “Take for yourself a scroll of a book and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you.”
As Jehudi read three or four columns (דְּלָתוֹת), the king cut them off with a scribe's knife and threw them into the fire, until the whole scroll was consumed.
“Take again another scroll and write on it all the former words.”
“A scroll of a book was in it, and he spread it before me, and it was written on the front and on the back.”
“Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel”; it was sweet as honey.
A flying scroll, twenty cubits long and ten wide: the curse going out over the land.
“Then I said, Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me.”
Psa 40:8 spoken of Christ coming into the world: “in the roll of the book (ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου) it is written of me, to do your will, O God.”
The quotation of Psa 40:8.

evidence.locator: Isa.34.4, כַסֵּפֶר → ὡς βιβλίον (the rolled heavens; the scroll is סֵפֶר there)

evidence.note: “A scroll written inside and on the back, sealed with seven seals”: as Ezk 2:10.

words.summary: A round hollow: a bowl, the bowl-shaped capitals of the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the bowl of the lampstand in Zechariah, the golden bowl of Ecclesiastes, and springs or basins of water in the Negev. Zec 4:2 spells it גֻּלָּהּ.

senses.definition: A round bowl: the oil-bowl on top of a lampstand, a golden bowl hung by a silver cord, and the round tops of the temple pillars.

evidence.note: “A lampstand all of gold, with its bowl (גֻּלָּהּ) on its top, and its seven lamps on it … and two olive trees by it, one on the right of the bowl.”
“Before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is broken”: of the end of a man's life.
“The two pillars and the bowls of the capitals that were on top of the pillars.”

senses.definition: Springs or basins of water, given with a dry field in the Negev.

evidence.note: Achsah: “You have given me the land of the Negev; give me also גֻּלֹּת מָיִם. And he gave her the upper גֻּלֹּת and the lower גֻּלֹּת.”

words.summary: The round of the head, the skull; and in numbering and levies, a head, one person. Its Aramaic form gave the place of the crucifixion its name, Golgotha, “which is called the place of a skull”.

senses.definition: The skull of a man.

evidence.note: “A woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.”
Of Jezebel “they found no more of her than the skull and the feet and the palms of the hands.”
They fastened Saul's head (גֻּלְגָּלְתּוֹ) in the house of Dagon.
“A place called Golgotha, which is called the place of a skull.”

senses.definition: A head counted, one person, in a census, a ration or a payment.

evidence.note: “By the number of names, every male, לְגֻלְגְּלֹתָם, head by head.”
“An omer לַגֻּלְגֹּלֶת”: a portion of manna for each person.
A beka a head, half a shekel, for everyone numbered.
Five shekels a head for the redemption of the firstborn.
The Levites numbered by their heads, thirty-eight thousand men.
“Aram. גָּלְגָּלְתָּא = Heb. גֻּלְגֹּלֶת, LXX κρανίον, Jg 9:53, IV Ki 9:35”.
“Golgotha, that is to say, the place of a skull (κρανίου τόπος)”: scripture's own interpretation of the name.
“The place called the place of a skull, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha.”
“The place that is called Skull (Κρανίον).”

words.summary: The root doubled: a thing that rolls round and round. A chariot's or cart's wheel, the wheel at the cistern, the whirling wheelwork beneath the cherubim, the whirl of the storm, and the dry thistle-head that rolls before the wind. Isa 28:28's גִּלְגַּל, a cart wheel, is the same word.

senses.definition: A wheel of a chariot or cart, or of the gear for drawing water.

evidence.note: “The hooves of their horses seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind.”
“At the rattling of his chariots, the rumbling of his wheels.”
“With chariot and wheel.”
“He drives the wheel (גִּלְגַּל) of his cart over it”: in threshing.
“The wheel broken at the cistern.”

senses.definition: The wheels beneath the cherubim in Ezekiel's vision, called together “the whirling”, from between which fire is taken.

evidence.note: “As for the wheels (אוֹפַנִּים), they were called in my hearing הַגַּלְגַּל.”
“Go in between the whirling wheels, underneath the cherub, and fill your hands with coals of fire.”

senses.definition: The whirl of a storm, and the dry, round head of a weed that the wind rolls away.

evidence.note: “The sound of your thunder was in the whirl; the lightnings lit up the world.”
“My God, make them like whirling dust (כַגַּלְגַּל), like chaff before the wind.”
The nations “chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and like whirling dust before the storm.”
“Setting on fire the wheel (τροχόν) of birth”: the Greek word only.

parallels.note: Wheel; Ezekiel's wheels are called the whirling.

words.gloss: account, cause: בִּגְלַל “on account of, for the sake of”
words.summary: Only with בְּ, as a preposition: בִּגְלַל, “on account of”, giving the cause of a blessing or a judgment. How it comes from rolling is not clear; Arabic uses its own jalal the same way, min jalalika “for your sake”, and Jewish Aramaic בִּגְלַל “on account of”, so the idiom itself is old and shared.

senses.gloss: on account of, because of, for the sake of
senses.definition: The cause or person for whose sake something is done, whether blessing or judgment.

evidence.note: “Yahweh blessed the Egyptian's house בִּגְלַל Joseph.”
“Yahweh has blessed me בִּגְלָלֶךָ, for your sake.”
“That it may go well with me for your sake.”
“Because of this thing Yahweh your God will bless you in all your work”: giving freely to the poor.
“Because of these abominations Yahweh your God is driving them out before you.”
“Yahweh was angry with me also on your account.”
“He will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam.”
“Because of Manasseh son of Hezekiah.”
“Therefore because of you Zion shall be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps.”

words.summary: Something round: a ring for hanging curtains, a rounded rod; and a circuit of land, a district, above all הַגָּלִיל, the district in the north, in the hill country of Naphtali, which Isaiah calls “Galilee of the nations” and where the light would first shine. The New Testament's Γαλιλαία is this word. No cognate yet ties its senses to the root: the link to rolling, a round thing and a circuit of land, rests on its form and on its sibling גְּלִילָה.

senses.definition: A ring or rounded rod of metal.

evidence.note: Hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings (גְּלִילֵי כֶסֶף) and marble pillars.
“His arms are rods (גְּלִילֵי) of gold set with beryl.”

senses.definition: The northern district of the land, in Naphtali, with its cities; called “Galilee of the nations”.

evidence.note: “Kedesh in Galilee (בַּגָּלִיל) in the hill country of Naphtali.”
Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities “in the land of Galilee”.
Tiglath-pileser took “Galilee, all the land of Naphtali” and exiled them.
“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali … the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, גְּלִיל הַגּוֹיִם.”
Isa 8:23–9:1 fulfilled when Jesus dwelt in Capernaum: “Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness saw a great light.”
“(Heb. הַגָּלִיל, the circle, district)”.
“Galilee of the nations”, quoting Isa 8:23.
“Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom of God.”
The eleven went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had appointed.

words.summary: The feminine of גָּלִיל: a circuit or region, in the plural “the regions of” a land or river; once a place, Geliloth on the border of Benjamin, called Gilgal at Jos 15:7. No cognate is recorded for it; Jewish Aramaic and Syriac גְּלִילָא are the place name only.

senses.definition: A region of land round about, as the regions of the Philistines or of the Jordan.

evidence.note: “All the regions (גְּלִילוֹת) of the Philistines and all the Geshurites.”
“The regions of the Jordan in the land of Canaan,” where the eastern tribes built the altar.
“Tyre and Sidon and all the regions of Philistia.”
“This water goes out to the eastern region (הַגְּלִילָה) and down into the Arabah, and enters the sea, and the waters will be healed.”

senses.definition: A place on the border of Benjamin and Judah, opposite the ascent of Adummim.

evidence.note: “It went out to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim.”
The same point on Judah's border, called Gilgal.

words.summary: A town north of Jerusalem, the home of Palti to whom Saul gave Michal, and on the line of the Assyrian advance in Isaiah. The name is the plural of גַּל, heaps (or springs); the text does not explain it. The count beside it includes three tokens of the noun גַּלִּים “heaps, waves”.

senses.definition: A town of Benjamin near Gibeah and Anathoth.

evidence.note: “Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.”
“Cry aloud, daughter of Gallim! … poor Anathoth!”

words.summary: Dung in lumps or balls, used dried as fuel and a picture of what is thrown out and burned. In the plural גֶּלְלֵי; 1Ki 14:10 has הַגָּלָל.

senses.definition: Dung of man or beast, burned as fuel and swept away.

evidence.note: “Bake it on human dung (בְּגֶלְלֵי צֵאַת הָאָדָם) in their sight.”
“I give you cow's dung instead of human dung (גֶּלְלֵי הָאָדָם), and you shall prepare your bread on it.”
“I will burn up the house of Jeroboam as one burns up dung (הַגָּלָל), until it is all gone.”
“Their blood poured out like dust, and their flesh like dung.”
The wicked “will perish forever like his own dung; those who saw him will say, Where is he?”

words.summary: Once, of door leaves that turn. BDB's key shares its other tokens (Est 1:6; Sng 5:14) with the noun, where they are entered. Its tie to the root rests on its form and one verse.

senses.definition: Of the leaves of a door, turning on pivots so that they fold.

evidence.note: “The two leaves of the one door were turning (גְּלִילִים), and the two leaves of the other door were turning.”

words.summary: The name Jacob gave the heap of stones raised as witness of his covenant with Laban: גַּל “heap” and עֵד “witness”, as the text itself says. Laban called it in Aramaic יְגַר שָׂהֲדוּתָא, the same meaning in other words.

senses.definition: The heap of stones in the hill country of Gilead set up as witness between Jacob and Laban.

evidence.note: “Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.”
“This heap is a witness between me and you today. Therefore its name was called Galeed.”

words.gloss: rolling: אֶבֶן גְּלָל “stones of rolling”, great stones
words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, only in אֶבֶן גְּלָל, the stones with which the second house was built: stones too great to carry, that had to be rolled into place.

senses.definition: Of building stones, great blocks moved by rolling.

evidence.note: “The house of the great God is being built with stones of rolling (אֶבֶן גְּלָל), and timber is laid in the walls.”
Cyrus' decree: “three courses of stones of rolling and one course of new timber.”

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, once: the wheels of the fiery throne of the Ancient of Days.

senses.definition: The wheels of a throne in Daniel's vision, burning fire.

evidence.note: “His throne was flames of fire, its wheels (גַּלְגִּלּוֹהִי) burning fire.”

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, once: the scroll of Cyrus' decree found in the archive at Ecbatana. The count beside it includes Zec 5:1, the Hebrew word of the same spelling.

senses.definition: A scroll kept in a royal archive, on which a decree was written.

evidence.note: “At Achmetha, in the fortress in the province of Media, a scroll (מְגִלָּה) was found, and in it was written: A record.”

cognates.note: The Hebrew verb's own sense in Neo-Assyrian.

evidence.locator: SEM001327 gll[roll]V: AKK002728 galālu[roll]V, ARM006008 GLL[roll]V, HEB001447 galal[roll]V

cognates.note: A stone noun of the root, as the Aramaic אֶבֶן גְּלָל.

cognates.gloss: column-base; an ornament in the shape of a column-base

cognates.note: A doubled form, like גַּלְגַּל and גִּלְגֵּל: motion to and fro and a round hollow ball. Its main sense is sounding and shaking, not rolling, so the link is possible only.

doctrine.statement: “Roll your way upon Yahweh, and trust in him, and he will act” (Psa 37:5); “roll your works to Yahweh, and your plans will be established” (Pro 16:3). To roll one's way on him is to trust him with it, and the psalm goes on, “rest in Yahweh and wait patiently for him … the meek shall inherit the land” (Psa 37:7, 11). In Psa 22 the sufferer's enemies throw the same words at him: “He rolled it to Yahweh; let him deliver him” (Psa 22:9). At the cross the chief priests said them of Jesus, “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he desires him” (Mat 27:43). He was not delivered from dying, but the psalm ends with Yahweh hearing him (Psa 22:25), and Hebrews puts its next words in Christ's mouth, “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Psa 22:23; Heb 2:12). Peter says, “God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death” (Act 2:24). Jesus prayed “to him who was able to save him out of death, and he was heard” (Heb 5:7), and committed himself “to him who judges righteously” (1Pe 2:23). From the verses: Jesus, a man, rolled his cause onto his Father and trusted him to the end; the mockers were wrong, for God did deliver him, out of death, by raising him. Those who commit their way to Yahweh are given the same hope.

Isaiah 34 is “the indignation of Yahweh against all the nations”: “the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll, and all their host shall fall”, and at once, “my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it comes down upon Edom” (Isa 34:2, 4–5). The heavens rolled up are in a judgment on the nations, and the sword that is “in the heavens” falls on a people on earth. Haggai uses the same picture: “I will shake the heavens and the earth, and I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms and destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations” (Hag 2:21–22). Revelation sets the scroll-like rolling of the heaven beside the kings of the earth, the great men and the commanders hiding from “the wrath of the Lamb” (Rev 6:14–17), and Hebrews explains Haggai's shaking as “the removal of the things that are shaken … that the things that cannot be shaken may remain”, and goes on, “we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Heb 12:26–28). From the verses: the heavens rolled up like a scroll are the ruling powers of the nations, taken away in Yahweh's judgment, to give place to the kingdom of God on earth (Dan 2:44).

Ezekiel names Israel's idols with this word thirty-nine times: idols set up in the heart (Ezk 14:3), the idols of Egypt Israel never forsook (Ezk 20:7–8), idols for which Yahweh scattered them among the nations (Ezk 36:18–19). Then the promise: “I will take you from the nations and gather you from all the countries and bring you into your own land. I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses, and from all your idols I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart” (Ezk 36:24–26). Again: “I will take the sons of Israel from the nations … and bring them to their own land, and make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king shall be king over them all … They shall not defile themselves any more with their idols … and David my servant shall be king over them” (Ezk 37:21–24). Paul quotes the end of that chapter, “I will dwell among them and be their God, and they shall be my people” (Ezk 37:27; 2Co 6:16), and sets it against idols. From the verses: the gathering is to the land itself, the mountains of Israel, under one king of David's line; the cleansing from idols is a new heart given to the nation, which had not happened when the prophecy was given and is still to come with the kingdom.

The waves are Yahweh's: he raises them (Psa 107:25), sets their bound, “here shall your proud waves be stayed” (Job 38:11; Jer 5:22), and stills them, “when its waves rise, you still them” (Psa 89:10); “he made the storm a calm, and their waves were still” (Psa 107:29). On the sea of Galilee the boat was covered by the waves, and Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm; the disciples asked, “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” (Mat 8:24–27; Mrk 4:37–41). Jesus answered the question of his power himself: “the Son can do nothing of himself, but only what he sees the Father doing” and “the Father who dwells in me does the works” (Jhn 5:19; 14:10); Peter preached “Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him” (Act 2:22). From the verses: what the psalms say only Yahweh does, the man Jesus did, because the Father did it through him; the stilling of the waves shows that the Son was sent with his Father's power, not that he was the Father.

note: Drafted 2026-11-18. Root key גלל; no existing entry used it. BDB keys assigned: c.cd.ao גִּלּוּל; c.cd.ar and b.bp.al Gilgal; c.cd.ab גַּל; c.cd.aa verb; c.cd.at מְגִלָּה; c.cd.ag and c.cd.af גֻּלָּה; c.cd.as גֻּלְגֹּלֶת; c.cd.ap and c.cd.aq גַּלְגַּל (Isa 28:28 גִּלְגַּל); c.cc.ab and b.ae.ag גָּלָל/בִּגְלַל; c.cd.al גָּלִיל noun; c.cd.am גְּלִילָה (c.cd.an גְּלִילוֹת lists the same tokens and is not named); c.cd.ac Gallim (shares 3 tokens with c.cd.ab); c.cd.ae and c.cd.ah גֵּל/גָּלָל dung; c.cd.ak the adjective (1Ki 6:34; its other tokens are the noun's); c.cd.ad and c.cf.ab Galeed; Aramaic xc.ag.ab גְּלָל, xc.ag.ac and xc.ae.ac גַּלְגַּל (Dan 7:9), xc.ag.ad and xm.aa.af מְגִלָּה (Ezr 6:2; the Hebrew c.cd.at also lists Ezr 6:2, and xc.ag.ad lists Zec 5:1 by spelling). Names: c.cd.ai Galal in names/galal.json, c.cd.aj Gilalai in names/gilalai.json. Left unassigned: c.cc.aa (BDB's root heading, “be great in rank”, from Arabic jalla; no Hebrew word shows that sense), c.bx.af, c.by.ad, c.ca.ah, m.aj.ak, xc.ae.ac's sibling cross-references with no tokens. Not this root: גִּלְעָד Gilead (BDB files it apart; its link to גַּל is a folk reading of Gen 31:47–48, not followed); גִּלְבֹּעַ Gilboa; מַגָּל sickle (Arabic minjal, a separate word). Psa 119:18 גַּל is גלה piel and stays in galah.json; galah.json's note already says Psa 119:22 and the no-stem גַּל tokens belong here. Open questions: (1) גִּלּוּלִים: whether it is “dung-things” (a scornful play on גֵּל, Ezk 4:12) or “rolled blocks”; no cognate names idols by this root, so it is left with no cognate and will show a negative balance. (2) Sng 4:12 גַּל נָעוּל: many read גַּן “garden” with some manuscripts; kept as “spring” beside גֻּלֹּת “springs”. (3) Psa 119:22 גַּל: tagged piel in the corpus, taken here as the qal imperative of this verb (galah.json agrees it is גלל). (4) The niphal וְיִגַּל of Amo 5:24 is entered as niphal “roll on” as the brief has it. Leads not followed: Phoenician 𐤂𐤋𐤂𐤋 glgl “wheel” (Wiktionary only; Krahmalkov not consulted); Ugaritic gl “bowl/cup” (DULAT not vendored); Ge'ez gll (Anderson–Moser give “lie”, not checked in Dillmann or Leslau); Akkadian aban galāla (a stone name like אֶבֶן גְּלָל, from CAD, not consulted); Syriac ܓܓܘܠܬܐ Golgotha (SEDRA lexeme 508, Mat 27:33; Mrk 15:22; Jhn 19:17), which the Peshitta glosses with ܩܪܩܦܬܐ “skull”, not recorded as a cognate. Arabic قُلَّة “jug”, linked by Wiktionary to גֻּלָּה, has q, not j, and is not a cognate. The doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review: the second reads the rolled-up heavens as the nations' ruling powers; the third reads Ezk 36–37 of a future gathering to the land under David's line.
